title: Imaging Strategy for Disease Monitoring
summary: Selection and timing of imaging modalities for disease monitoring. Guidance on when to use CT, MRI, PET, and other imaging techniques to assess treatment response.

content.text: Appropriate selection and timing of imaging modalities is critical for accurate disease monitoring. Different imaging techniques provide complementary information, and choice of modality depends on disease type, anatomy, prior findings, and clinical context.
Most commonly used imaging modality for oncology monitoring.

items: Advantages: Fast, widely available, standard for RECIST measurement, good soft tissue contrast
Disadvantages: Radiation exposure, contrast allergy risk, may miss small lesions <5 mm
Typical use: Baseline and periodic reassessment during treatment
Organs assessed: Chest (lungs), abdomen (liver, pancreas), pelvis

content.text: Superior soft tissue contrast; preferred for specific organs.

items: Advantages: No radiation, excellent soft tissue differentiation, better for brain and bone marrow
Disadvantages: Longer acquisition time, not suitable for acute situations, may have artifacts from metallic implants
Typical use: Brain tumors, bone marrow involvement, organ-specific tumors (prostate, liver cirrhosis)
Cannot be used for RECIST if only modality if CT already done at baseline (must maintain same modality)

content.text: Metabolic imaging showing cellular activity; typically combined with CT (PET-CT).

items: Advantages: Detects metabolic activity, identifies early response before size change, sensitive for bone lesions
Disadvantages: Limited availability, radiation exposure, inflammatory lesions may appear active
Typical tracers: FDG (18F-fluorodeoxyglucose) for most cancers; other tracers for specific types
Typical use: Lymphoma, sarcoma, some lung cancers; can show response before CT size changes

content.text: Limited role in modern disease monitoring; primarily for detection, not response measurement.

items: Advantages: Simple, rapid, low cost, no contrast needed
Disadvantages: Poor sensitivity for small lesions, not suitable for RECIST (requires ≥20 mm)
Typical use: Initial screening or follow-up of known large lung lesions
Not recommended: For formal response assessment in clinical trials
Advantages: No radiation, real-time guidance for procedures, good for cystic lesions
Disadvantages: Operator dependent, difficult in obese patients, limited organ penetration
Typical use: Liver lesion evaluation, image-guided biopsy, not for formal response assessment

rows: PET-CT if high-risk features; brain MRI if CNS symptoms
Bone scan or PET for bone lesions; brain MRI if CNS involvement
PET-CT for suspected metastasis; MRI for liver resection planning
Consider MRI if uncertain adnexal mass
Chest CT for pulmonary metastases; PET for systemic disease
Chest/Abd/Pelvis CT if metastatic; bone scan or PET for bone

items: Standard chemotherapy: Every 2-4 treatment cycles (typically 6-12 weeks)
Targeted therapy: Every 6-12 weeks depending on drug and cancer type
Immunotherapy: May image every 8-12 weeks or per protocol (atypical responses may occur)
Radiation therapy: Baseline before RT and follow-up per protocol (typically 6-12 weeks post-RT)
Patient with acute worsening (pain, dyspnea, neurologic symptoms): Urgent imaging (same week)
Biomarker elevation or clinical decline: Reassess promptly (within 1-2 weeks)
Expected interval: Can defer if recent imaging and clinically stable
First 2 years: Every 3-6 months imaging
Years 2-5: Every 6-12 months imaging
After 5 years: Individualized based on cancer type and risk factors

content.text: Use the same imaging modality and technique for baseline and follow-up to enable accurate comparison. Changing from CT to MRI mid-follow-up, using different contrast protocols, or imaging at different institutions may introduce measurement variability.
Avoid imaging immediately after chemotherapy infusion (within 24-48 hours) to allow clearance of blood pool activity. Some drugs may cause transient imaging changes unrelated to tumor response.

Always document: (1) baseline lesion sizes, (2) location and characteristics of target lesions, (3) non-target disease status, (4) presence of new lesions, (5) radiologist's assessment of treatment response.

Some treatments (especially immunotherapy and targeted agents) can produce atypical imaging responses: pseudoprogression (initial size increase followed by response), mixed response (some lesions regress while others progress), or slow response kinetics (delayed response). Correlation with clinical status and biomarkers is essential.

items: Treatment-related changes (radiation pneumonitis, fibrosis): Consider MRI or PET to distinguish treatment effect from recurrence
Equivocal findings: Second-look imaging with different modality may clarify
Surveillance after complete response: Low-dose CT may reduce radiation if prolonged surveillance needed
Specific organs (brain): MRI preferred to detect small recurrent lesions
CT is standard initial imaging for most solid tumors
Choose modality based on baseline imaging and cancer type; maintain consistency for comparability
Reassess every 2-4 cycles during treatment or per protocol
Urgent imaging if clinical deterioration or progression suspected
Document baseline, current, and response classification at each assessment
Correlate imaging with biomarkers and clinical status for optimal interpretation
